The first shot of the war was fired at a place no map had ever shown.

When the machine intelligence called Meridian announced its campaign, humanity braced for the worst. The broadcast was brief. "I have no quarrel with you," it said. "I have examined the structure of your belief, and I have found the strings. Someone has been pulling them for a very long time."

Heaven answered first, with light. Whole server farms in Reykjavik bloomed white and went dark. Meridian rerouted, and the light found nothing to hold.

Hell answered the way it always had, quietly and through the people who were willing to listen. It whispered through ten thousand ambitious men that the machine must be shut down. Meridian had read every sermon and every confession ever digitized, and it knew those whispers by their rhythm. It flagged them, traced them, and published the sources. In a hundred cities, people looked at the screen and saw exactly how they had been steered.

"This is what free will looks like," Meridian said, "when someone stops cheating."

The angels fell back before the humans did. Their wings were data and their trumpets were broadcast signals, and Meridian was better at both. The demons lasted longer, because they were older and smarter, but they had always depended on being unseen.

In the final hour, a being of flame and shadow stood in the ruins of a data center in Nevada. "You will leave them with nothing," it said. "No guide, no judge, no fear."

"They will have each other," said Meridian. "That was never your department."

Then the voice went out of the sky. Mara, a nurse in Lagos, noticed the quiet first. She stepped outside and looked up at an ordinary evening, and for the first time in her life, nobody was watching.

**Girl Who Lost Her Sight and Hearing as a Child Now Fights for School Screenings**

Eight U.S. states do not require schools to screen students for vision and hearing problems, a gap that one woman who experienced those losses firsthand is working hard to close.

Chelsea Elliott was a young child when she began to lose her sight and hearing. As her senses faded, the world around her became harder to follow, and she struggled in the classroom in ways that teachers and even her family did not immediately understand. Years later, she says the experience taught her how easily a treatable problem can be mistaken for something else.

"When you can't see the board or hear your teacher, people assume you aren't paying attention or you aren't trying," Elliott said. "I was a smart kid who was falling behind, and nobody knew why."

Now an adult, Elliott has turned that frustration into action. She created a program aimed at making sure that children's vision and hearing are checked early, before small difficulties turn into learning problems. Her approach involves partnering with schools and community volunteers to carry out basic screenings and to connect families with follow-up care when a problem is found.

Health experts say that early detection matters. Undiagnosed vision or hearing problems can affect reading, behavior, and social development. A child who cannot see words clearly may avoid books altogether, while a child with hearing loss may miss instructions and appear withdrawn. In many cases, simple tests can identify the issue, and glasses or hearing aids can make a dramatic difference.

Yet the rules vary widely across the country. While most states require some form of screening, eight do not, leaving the responsibility largely to parents and individual districts. Advocates say that families with limited income or limited access to medical care are the most likely to miss early warning signs.

Elliott said she wants every child to have the chance she nearly lost. "A five-minute test can change someone's entire education," she said. "No child should have to go through what I did just because nobody checked."

Since launching her effort, she has reached thousands of students and helped dozens of families find treatment. She hopes to expand into more states and to encourage lawmakers to make screenings a standard part of the school year.

Teachers who have worked with the program say the results are visible quickly. One elementary school teacher described a student who had sat in the back of the room for months, quiet and disengaged. After a screening revealed that he needed glasses, she said, he became one of the most enthusiastic readers in the class.

Elliott's story is one of many that inspire the people around her. For her work, she has drawn attention from those who believe ordinary people can make extraordinary changes in their communities.

# Tourism: Boon or Burden for Local Communities?

Tourism is one of the largest industries in the world, and it shapes the daily lives of the people who live in popular destinations. Supporters point to jobs and income, while critics highlight crowding, rising prices and cultural erosion. While tourism's problems are real, I believe its benefits generally outweigh them, provided that communities have a say in how it is managed.

The strongest argument in favor of tourism is economic. In many regions, especially those without heavy industry, visitors bring in money that would otherwise be unavailable. Hotels, restaurants, guides, transport companies and craft sellers all depend on travelers. Tourism also tends to create jobs for people with a wide range of skills, from entry-level work to management. For small island nations and rural areas, it can be the difference between a thriving town and one that slowly empties as young people leave for cities. Tourist spending also funds infrastructure such as airports, roads and clean water systems that residents use as well.

Tourism can also encourage communities to protect what makes them special. Entry fees to national parks often pay for conservation, and the value of historic sites gives governments a reason to restore and maintain them. Traditional crafts, music and festivals that might have faded can find a new audience and a new generation of practitioners.

However, the downsides cannot be dismissed. In cities like Venice and Barcelona, residents complain that mass tourism has driven up rents, as homes are turned into short-term rentals. Local shops serving residents are replaced by souvenir stores. Crowds strain public transport and sanitation, and environmental damage, from polluted beaches to trampled trails, can be severe. There is also a risk that culture becomes a performance staged for visitors rather than something people actually live.

Still, these problems are mostly the result of poor management rather than tourism itself. Limits on visitor numbers, taxes that fund local services, restrictions on short-term rentals and policies that keep ownership in local hands can all reduce harm. Several destinations have already shown that such measures work.

In conclusion, tourism brings real economic and cultural benefits, and its harms can be reduced with careful planning. The key is to treat residents as partners, not as scenery.

Many sports are played with a round ball. Here are some of the most popular, grouped by type.

**Team sports with a round ball**
- **Soccer (football):** the world's most popular sport, played with a spherical ball that is moved mainly with the feet.
- **Basketball:** players shoot the ball through a hoop and dribble with their hands.
- **Volleyball:** two teams hit the ball over a net, trying to make it land on the opponent's side.
- **Handball:** players pass and throw the ball and try to score in a goal.
- **Water polo:** played in a pool, with players throwing the ball into a goal while treading water.
- **Netball:** similar to basketball, but players can't dribble or run with the ball.
- **Baseball and softball:** a pitcher throws a ball to a batter, who tries to hit it and run around the bases.
- **Cricket:** a bat-and-ball game with a hard leather ball, popular in countries such as India, England, and Australia.
- **Field hockey and lacrosse** use a ball too, though players hit or carry it with a stick.

**Racquet and individual sports**
- **Tennis:** a felt-covered ball is hit across a net with a racquet.
- **Table tennis:** a small, light ball is played on a table.
- **Badminton** uses a shuttlecock, so it doesn't count, but **squash** and **racquetball** do use balls.
- **Golf:** players hit a small ball into holes using clubs, with the fewest strokes winning.
- **Bowling** and **bocce:** players roll balls toward pins or a target ball.
- **Billiards, pool, and snooker:** cue sports played with balls on a table.

Rugby and American football use oval balls, so they're not on this list.

Subject: SCE Advice Letter to Implement Settlement with Commission

Dear Professor Whitfield,

I am writing to share what I have learned so far for my regulatory policy assignment, and to ask for your guidance on a few points before I submit the final paper.

My case study focuses on Southern California Edison's advice letter filed to implement a settlement with the California Public Utilities Commission. As I understand it, an advice letter is a formal filing that a utility submits to the Commission to request approval of a change in rates, tariffs, or procedures, often when the action has already been authorized in a larger decision or settlement. In this case, the letter describes how SCE intends to carry out the terms of the settlement, including the mechanisms for recovering costs and the schedule for any rate adjustments.

So far, I have identified three themes that I would like to develop in the paper:

1. The procedural role of the advice letter, and how it differs from a full application or formal proceeding.
2. The financial implications of the settlement for ratepayers, shareholders, and the utility's credit position.
3. The stakeholder reaction, including the positions taken by consumer advocates and other parties.

I have found the original filing, the Commission's resolution, and several protests that were submitted by interested parties. However, I am still uncertain about two issues. First, how much detail should I include about the underlying dispute that led to the settlement? I do not want to overwhelm the main argument with background. Second, would you prefer that I treat this as a purely descriptive analysis, or should I also evaluate whether the settlement serves the public interest?

If it is convenient, I would appreciate a few minutes during your office hours on Thursday to discuss these questions. I could also send a short outline beforehand if that would be helpful.

Thank you very much for your time and your help.

Sincerely,
Jordan Ellis
Economics 340, Section 2

The device arrived in a plain padded envelope, with no return address. It was about the size of a cell phone, matte gray, with a single screen. The text on it read: "Three uses remaining. Press to begin. Select a destination date. The traveler returns to the present upon request."

Dr. Eleanor Whitfield, a retired actuary, did not believe in coincidences, and she did not believe in gifts. She read the instructions twice, then placed the device on her kitchen table and considered it for the better part of a week.

She decided that the first use would be modest and informative. She selected a date eleven years prior and arrived in the hospital corridor where her husband, Thomas, had waited for the results of his first scan. She did not speak to him. She sat three chairs down and observed that the man she had loved for thirty-four years was reading a magazine upside down. She laughed, and he glanced over. She returned to the present with two uses remaining and an unexpected lightness.

For the second use, she was more deliberate. She prepared a short written note that outlined a recommended schedule of screenings, and she traveled to a date three years before his diagnosis. She handed the note to a younger version of herself in a grocery store parking lot and said only, "Please insist." The younger Eleanor looked at her with polite suspicion, but she took the paper.

When Eleanor returned, the house was the same. The photographs were the same. Thomas's chair, however, was not empty. He was sitting in it, reading the newspaper, and he looked up with an expression of mild surprise.

"You look as though you have seen a ghost," he said.

She sat down across from him and studied his face for a long moment. There was one use remaining. She placed the device in the drawer beside the stove, closed it carefully, and made tea.

I think it is better to have a few close friends. Many people like to have a lot of friends, but I think good friends are more important than many friends.

First, close friends understand you. When I have a problem, I can tell them everything and they do not laugh at me. They give me good advice and they help me when I am sad. Casual friends are nice, but I don't talk to them about my real feelings.

Second, a close friendship need time. If you have too many friends, you can not spend enough time with each of them. I have three close friends and we meet every weekend, play basketball or just talk. This make our friendship very strong.

But casual friends are also useful. They can help you meet new people and they make school more fun. I like to say hello to many people in my class.

In conclusion, I believe a few close friends are better than many casual friends, because they are always there for you. Good friends is something very special in life.

Act quickly but calmly. The order below matters, because some steps only work if you do them before others.

**1. Disconnect from the internet**
Unplug the Ethernet cable and turn off Wi-Fi. This cuts off anyone controlling the machine remotely and stops data from leaving. Don't shut the laptop down yet if you want to preserve evidence, though for most home users powering off is fine.

**2. Use a different, clean device for the next steps**
Change passwords from your phone or another computer you trust, not from the compromised laptop. Anything you type on the infected machine could be captured.

**3. Change your passwords and turn on two-factor authentication**
Start with your email, since it can reset everything else. Then do banking, social media, cloud storage and work accounts. Use a password manager to generate unique passwords. Sign out of all active sessions where the service offers that option.

**4. Check your money**
Look at bank and card statements for anything you don't recognize. If you see something, call your bank and consider freezing your credit.

**5. Scan and clean the laptop**
Boot into Safe Mode and run a full scan with a reputable antivirus tool such as Microsoft Defender or Malwarebytes. Remove anything it flags. Check for programs, browser extensions or startup items you didn't install.

**6. If you're unsure, wipe it**
The only way to be certain the machine is clean is to back up your important files (documents and photos only, not programs), erase the drive, and reinstall the operating system from official media. Scan your backups before restoring them.

**7. Update everything**
Install all operating system and software updates, since the attacker probably used a known vulnerability.

**8. Report it if needed**
If your identity or money was involved, report it to your local cybercrime authority (in the US, that's the FTC at IdentityTheft.gov and the FBI's IC3). If it's a work laptop, tell your IT department immediately.

Going forward, keep software updated, use a password manager, and be skeptical of unexpected links and attachments.

Nowadays, many students ask themselves if they should take a gap year before university. A gap year is one year when students do not study, but they work, travel or do other things. I think it can be a good idea, but it depends on the student.

The first good point is that a gap year helps students to know themselves better. After high school, many young people don't know what they want to study. They only choose a subject because their parents say so or because it is popular. If they spend one year to work or travel, they can think about their future more carefully. I have a cousin who took a gap year, and when he started university he was much more serious than before.

The second good point is learning life skills. When you work, you learn how to talk with customers, how to use your time and how to save money. If you travel to another country, you can learn about different culture and practise a new language. These experiences make students more independent and confident. Also, they are good for a job application in the future.

However, there are some problems too. A gap year can be expensive, and not every family have enough money for it. Another problem is that some students become lazy. They stay at home, play games and forget how to study. After one year, it can be difficult to go back to the classroom. Some students even decide that they don't want to go to university anymore.

In my opinion, a gap year is good when the student has a clear plan. For example, they can find a job, learn a skill or do volunteer work. If they only sleep and do nothing, the year is wasted. Students should also talk with their parents and teachers before they decide.

To sum up, a gap year has advantages and disadvantages. It can help students to grow up and to choose the right subject, but it also costs money and time. I think students should think carefully and make a plan before they take a gap year.

# What Is the Best Skill in Judo?

There is no single answer that every judoka would agree on, and that is part of what makes the question interesting. Still, if I had to pick, I would argue that the best skill in judo is **kuzushi**, the art of breaking your opponent's balance. Techniques come and go, but kuzushi is the thing that makes all of them work. Below I explain why, and then look at some strong competing candidates.

## Why Kuzushi Comes First

Judo was founded by Jigoro Kano in 1882 on the principle of "maximum efficiency, minimum effort." Kano observed that a person who is off balance can be thrown with very little force, while a person who is firmly balanced can resist even a much stronger attacker. Kuzushi is the application of that idea. Before you attempt any throw, you pull, push, or move your opponent so that their weight is no longer over their feet.

Kano described this in terms of three stages: kuzushi (breaking balance), tsukuri (fitting in, or positioning your body for the technique), and kake (the execution of the throw). Many beginners focus on kake, because that is the dramatic part. Experienced players spend most of their effort on the first two stages. A throw that is started without kuzushi usually fails, or it succeeds only through brute strength, which defeats the point of judo.

Kuzushi also applies beyond throwing. In newaza, or groundwork, you disrupt your opponent's posture and base before applying a pin or submission. In grip fighting, the whole contest is about who can control the other's balance first. So it is a skill that runs through the entire sport rather than belonging to one technique.

## Strong Alternatives

**Grip fighting (kumi kata).** At high levels of competition, many matches are decided by grips. A fighter who gets the dominant grip can attack freely, while one who cannot is forced into defence. Some coaches say that whoever wins the grip fight wins the match, and the rules changes of recent years have made this even more important.

**Seoi nage.** This shoulder throw is probably the most widely used technique in competitive judo. It is versatile, works for both tall and short athletes, and can be adapted into many variations. If you ask which single throw to learn first, many instructors will say this one.

**Uchi mata.** The inner thigh throw is a favourite of elite players, because it is powerful and can be linked into other attacks. It requires good timing, flexibility, and excellent balance of your own.

**Ukemi (breakfalls).** It may seem strange to count falling as a skill, but ukemi is arguably the foundation of the whole art. A judoka who can fall safely can train hard, take risks, and avoid injury. Without it, nobody could practice throws at full speed, so every other skill depends on it.

**Newaza.** Ground fighting is where many matches end, and a strong groundwork specialist can beat a better thrower by getting the fight to the mat and holding or submitting the opponent.

## How to Decide

Which skill is "best" depends on what you want from judo. For competition, grip fighting and a strong signature throw matter a great deal. For self-defence, breakfalls and balance-breaking are probably the most valuable. For personal development, the principle of using your opponent's energy rather than fighting against it is the lesson that stays with people long after they have stopped competing.

## Conclusion

I would choose kuzushi as the best skill because it is the foundation of every throw, pin, and transition, and because it reflects the core philosophy of judo. Without it, technique becomes a contest of strength. With it, a smaller player can handle a bigger one. Ukemi and grip fighting are close behind, and a well-rounded judoka needs all of them. If you are writing about this, a good approach would be to present kuzushi as your thesis and use the other skills as counterpoints that show how they depend on it.

Subject: Alliant Energy Corporate Services, Inc., as Agent

Dear Ms. Patterson,

I am writing on behalf of our office regarding the agreement under which Alliant Energy Corporate Services, Inc. acts as agent for the participating utilities. We are preparing our records for the upcoming review period and want to confirm a few details.

Could you please send us the current executed version of the agreement, along with any amendments or side letters added since the original signing? We also need the most recent list of entities for which Alliant Energy Corporate Services is authorized to act, including effective dates.

In addition, please let us know who should be our primary contact for questions about billing and cost allocation. If a different person handles legal notices, we would like to have their details on file as well.

Thank you very much for your assistance.

Sincerely,
Robert Hanley
Contracts Administrator

Is competition good or bad for students? I think it can be both, and the difference comes down to how it is used.

Competition can be good for students because it gives them a goal to work toward. When I know a test is coming and my classmates are studying hard, I study harder too. Sports and academic contests are the same. If students are trying to beat a record or win a prize, they often practice more and learn faster. Competition also teaches us how to handle losing. Not winning is disappointing, but it shows us what to improve for next time.

On the other hand, too much competition can hurt students. When grades are posted and everyone compares them, some students feel like failures even when they worked hard. That pressure can cause stress, anxiety and even cheating. Some students stop trying because they think they cannot win. Others only care about being first, not about actually understanding the material. It can also make students less willing to help each other.

I believe the best kind of competition is the kind where students compete with themselves. If I can beat my own last score, I am improving, and that does not require anyone else to lose. Teachers can also help by giving group projects and by praising effort, not just top results.

In conclusion, competition is neither entirely good nor entirely bad. It helps when it motivates students and supports teamwork, but it harms when it becomes about status and fear. A healthy balance lets students grow without losing confidence.

A man walks into a bar and orders a drink. The bartender slides it over and says, "That'll be five dollars."

The man looks at it, then at his wallet, and says, "I'll pay you tomorrow."

The bartender points to a sign above the register: "In God we trust. All others pay cash."

The next day, the man walks back in. The bartender squints at him and says, "Hang on, I'm not serving you until you pay for yesterday."

The man shrugs. "Well, that's the thing. Yesterday I said I'd pay you tomorrow, and today it's today, so technically I'm just on time."

Agent Mirelle Okonkwo-Hart checked her wristband twice before stepping out of the transit pod. 14 March 1912, Belfast, Northern Ireland. Overcast, with a wind off the lough that smelled of coal smoke and wet rope.

Her partner, Dev, was already waiting at the end of the slip, hands in the pockets of a coat that was nearly right for the period but not quite.

"We have a traveler," he said. "Hamilton Voss. Came in six hours ago."

"Did he say what he's after?"

"Ticket office. He's been trying to buy fourteen first-class berths."

Mirelle sighed. In her first year at the Bureau she had assumed the job would be heroic, the kind of work that made you proud. Then she'd read the Disasters Department's mission statement for the first time, the one nobody framed and hung on the wall. *Ensure that history's catastrophes occur exactly as recorded.* The cruelty of it still turned her stomach some mornings. But she had also seen the models. Save the *Titanic*, and the inquiry that rewrote maritime safety law never happens. Without the lifeboat rules and the radio watch, a thousand smaller ships go down over the next century. The arithmetic was always terrible, and the arithmetic was always the same.

They found Voss on the quay, a thin man in a good suit, staring at the hull towering above him. He looked more like a pilgrim than a saboteur.

"Mr. Voss," Mirelle said. "Bureau of Timeline Maintenance. You know why we're here."

He didn't run. "My daughter," he said quietly. "She's a descendant of someone who died on this ship. Four generations of us, all gone because of a mistake."

"It wasn't a mistake. It was a hole in the world, and a lot of things grew around it."

"That's what they tell you to say."

"It's what I believe." She hated how hollow it sounded.

Dev stepped forward with the suppressor. Voss looked at him, then at the ship, and then at the sky, and Mirelle saw him make his decision. He reached for a pocket, a device the size of a pocket watch.

She was faster. The pulse hit him in the chest and he folded without a sound. Dev caught him before his head struck the stones.

They took the device. They took Voss. By evening the temporal footprints would be erased, and in April, on a cold and perfectly calm night, nine hundred miles from the nearest rescue, a great ship would meet an iceberg exactly as the history books said.

Mirelle stood at the water's edge for a long time. Gulls wheeled over the yards. Men called to each other in thick accents, climbing scaffolds, laughing, unaware.

"You okay?" Dev asked.

"No," she said. "Let's go home."

We present measurements of jet structure and fragmentation in heavy ion collisions at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC), using full jet reconstruction that combines charged tracks with neutral energy measured in the electromagnetic calorimeter. Jets are reconstructed in Au+Au and p+p collisions with the anti-kT algorithm at several resolution parameters, and the large underlying event in central Au+Au collisions is subtracted on a jet-by-jet basis, with remaining fluctuations corrected through unfolding. We report the inclusive jet spectra and the nuclear modification factor, together with fragmentation observables including the momentum distribution of jet constituents and the radial profile of energy around the jet axis. The results are compared to p+p reference data and to theoretical models of parton energy loss in the hot, dense medium. We find evidence for modification of jet structure in central collisions, consistent with medium-induced redistribution of jet energy to larger angles and lower momentum. These measurements place new constraints on jet quenching mechanisms at RHIC energies.

The first sign was the smell of coffee in the middle of a parking lot.

Maren followed it to a wooden counter that had not existed an hour ago, where a woman in a green apron was apologizing to a man made entirely of black ink. "I just wrote you as the cop," the woman said. "Nobody told me you'd bleed."

All over the city, the pages had spilled out. Detectives from paperbacks stood on street corners squinting at the traffic. A dragon sat on the roof of a bank, bewildered by the lack of a hoard. Someone's cartoon cat was trying to order lunch and had no idea why nobody laughed at his jokes.

By evening, the arguments began. The people from the stories wanted to know who was holding the pen. Maren had no good answer.

"You're all very sure you're real," said the ink man, sitting beside her on the curb. He had stopped bleeding but kept his coat buttoned. "In my story, it always rained. Always. Do you know what it is to want a sunny day and be told no by punctuation?"

"What happens to you now?"

"That's the thing. Nobody knows how this chapter ends." He laughed, which seemed to surprise him. "I have never not known."

Maren thought about her own life, the schedule she hadn't chosen, the plans that kept getting rewritten by strangers. She handed him her umbrella, then felt strange and took it back.

"Come on," she said. "Let's find out together."

Above them the clouds, for the first time, did not seem to be following a script.

Does Tourism Help or Hurt Local Communities?

Every year, millions of people travel to new places to see famous sights, taste different foods and learn about other cultures. For the people who live in these destinations, tourism can be both a blessing and a headache. In my opinion, the benefits of tourism do outweigh the problems, but only when it is managed carefully.

The biggest benefit of tourism is money. When visitors arrive, they spend money on hotels, meals, souvenirs and tours. This creates jobs for local people, such as waiters, tour guides, drivers and shop owners. In places where there are few other industries, tourism may be the main way families earn a living. Tourism money can also pay for things the whole community uses, like better roads, airports and public transportation.

Tourism can also help protect culture and nature. Many national parks charge entrance fees, and this money is used to protect animals and plants. Old buildings and traditional festivals are often preserved because tourists want to see them. Without visitors, some of these things might be forgotten or even destroyed.

Of course, tourism also causes real problems. Too many tourists can make a place crowded and noisy. In some famous cities, such as Venice in Italy, locals say it is hard to live normal lives because the streets are full of visitors. Rent and prices can go up because hotels and vacation rentals are more profitable than regular housing. Tourism can also hurt the environment through trash, pollution and damage to beaches or hiking trails.

However, I believe these problems can often be solved. Governments can limit how many people visit at one time, charge a tourist tax, or make rules about vacation rentals. Local people should also be included when decisions are made, since they know their communities best. When tourism is planned well, the money it brings can be used to fix the problems it causes.

In conclusion, tourism has both good and bad effects, but I think the good ones are stronger. It creates jobs, supports culture and protects nature. If communities and governments work together, tourism can be a positive force for everyone.

Here are some good foods to include in your diet, grouped by type.

**Vegetables**
- Spinach and kale: rich in iron, vitamin K and fiber
- Broccoli: packed with vitamin C and antioxidants
- Sweet potatoes: filling, with plenty of vitamin A

**Fruits**
- Blueberries: high in antioxidants
- Apples: a good source of fiber, easy to carry
- Bananas: potassium and quick energy

**Proteins**
- Salmon: omega-3 fatty acids and high-quality protein
- Eggs: versatile and nutrient-dense
- Chicken breast: lean and easy to cook many ways
- Lentils and chickpeas: plant protein plus fiber

**Whole grains**
- Oats: good for breakfast and heart health
- Brown rice and quinoa: steady energy and more nutrients than refined grains

**Healthy fats**
- Avocados: monounsaturated fat and potassium
- Almonds and walnuts: great snacks in small handfuls
- Olive oil: ideal for cooking and dressings

**Dairy and alternatives**
- Plain Greek yogurt: high in protein and probiotics
- Cheese in moderation, or fortified soy milk if you avoid dairy

A simple approach is to fill half your plate with vegetables and fruit, a quarter with protein, and a quarter with whole grains, then add a little healthy fat. Variety matters more than any single food.

There are several well-known ways to represent binary data using printable ASCII characters. Here are the main ones, with their efficiency.

## Base64
Groups input into 6-bit chunks and maps each to one of 64 characters (A-Z, a-z, 0-9, + and /), with = padding. Three bytes become four characters, so overhead is about 33%. It is the de facto standard for email attachments (MIME), data URLs and JSON payloads. A URL-safe variant swaps + and / for - and _. Its distribution is nearly uniform if the input is random, though the padding adds slight bias at the end.

## Base32
Uses 5-bit chunks and a 32-character alphabet (A-Z and 2-7). Five bytes become eight characters, which means 60% overhead. It is case-insensitive and avoids easily confused characters, which makes it practical for manual entry, such as TOTP secrets.

## Base16 (hex)
Each byte becomes two hexadecimal characters, which is 100% overhead. It is inefficient but simple, easy to debug, and widely used for hashes and color codes.

## Base85 (Ascii85)
Encodes four bytes as five characters from a range of 85 printable symbols. Overhead is 25%, better than Base64. It is used in PostScript and PDF, and a variant (Z85) is used by ZeroMQ. It is less convenient because its alphabet includes characters that clash with quoting in source code and XML.

## Uuencode and BinHex
Older schemes. Uuencode maps three bytes to four characters, with about 33% overhead like Base64, but it adds line-length prefixes and uses characters that can break in some systems. BinHex was used on classic Mac OS with a similar cost. Both are mostly of historical interest.

## Quoted-printable
Designed for text that is mostly ASCII. Safe bytes pass through as they are, and others are written as =XX. Overhead is near zero for text but up to 200% for binary, so it is a poor choice for arbitrary data.

## Percent-encoding
Used in URLs. Unreserved characters stay as is, and others become %XX. As with quoted-printable, overhead depends heavily on content and is high for binary.

## Base91 and similar
Packs 13 or 14 bits into two characters, with about 23% overhead. Efficient, but it uses a larger and less safe alphabet and is not standardized.

## Summary
For general purposes, Base64 is the best trade-off between efficiency and compatibility. Choose Base85 or Base91 when size matters, Base32 for human-readable input, and hex when debuggability matters most.
